title: Coming back when called
summary: From turning to their name to coming back on a long line with mild distractions.

stages.title: Turning to their name
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog looks your way when they hear their name, said once.
stages.whyItMatters: Every recall starts with your dog turning towards you. A name that always pays off is the first step of coming back.
stages.everydayPractice: Say their name once when they are already about to look at you, and reward the look.

gate.summary: Orients to you within 2 seconds of their name, said once at normal volume, in low distraction.
gate.ownerCheck: In a quiet room, does {dog} look at you within a couple of seconds of hearing their name once?

stages.ifGateFails: Shorten the game, go somewhere quieter and use a reward your dog loves. Say the name once, not again and again.
stages.maintenance: Reward a few name responses on ordinary days, especially when your dog chooses to look at you.

lessons.title: Why their name comes first
lessons.body: Every recall starts with your dog turning towards you. Before their name means anything, reward every glance they give you on their own. Then their name becomes the sound that says "look at me, something good is coming".

lessons.title: The name game
lessons.aim: A few short rounds: say {dog}'s name once, and reward the look.

lessons.title: Say it once
lessons.body: If {dog} doesn't look, don't say their name again and again. Repeating it teaches them it can be ignored. Move a little, make a small noise, or make it easier, then reward the look.

lessons.title: Catch it in real life
lessons.body: Today, when {dog} is already about to look at you, say their name once and reward the look. Three times is plenty.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} doesn't look when you say their name. What helps most?
options: Say it again, louder
Make it easier: move a little or go somewhere quieter, then reward the look
Wait until they're bored, then try
lessons.explanation: Repeating the name teaches your dog to tune it out. Making it easier gets the look you can reward.

stages.title: Coming back nearby
stages.whatItMeans: One recall word, and your dog comes to you in a quiet, enclosed space or on a long line.
stages.whyItMatters: A recall that always pays off at home is the base for every place after it.
stages.everydayPractice: Call once when your dog is already heading your way, and make arriving worth it.

gate.summary: Returns to arm's reach on a 5 m long line, to a single cue, in low distraction.
gate.ownerCheck: On a 5 metre long line somewhere quiet, does {dog} come back to arm's reach when called once?

stages.ifGateFails: Go back to the name game and shorten the distance. Don't repeat the recall word if your dog is unlikely to come; go and get them calmly instead.
stages.maintenance: A few rewarded recalls on ordinary walks each week, and never call only to end the fun.

lessons.title: One word, always worth it
lessons.body: Pick one recall word, like "come" or "here", and make sure everyone at home uses the same one. Call once, step back, and make arriving the best thing that happens: a happy voice and a treat your dog loves.

lessons.title: Recall in a quiet place
lessons.aim: Indoors or in the garden: name, recall word, step away, and celebrate when {dog} arrives.

lessons.title: Give them five seconds
lessons.body: After you call, give {dog} at least five seconds to respond before doing anything else. If they're unlikely to come, don't repeat the word: go and get them calmly instead, so the word keeps its meaning.

lessons.title: Late is still a win
lessons.body: However slowly {dog} comes back, greet them warmly and reward them. Telling a dog off when they arrive teaches them that coming back isn't safe.

lessons.title: Call when they're coming anyway
lessons.body: When {dog} is already heading your way at home, say the recall word once and reward them when they reach you.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} finally comes back after taking their time. What do you do?
options: Reward them warmly
Tell them off so they're quicker next time
Ignore them
lessons.explanation: Coming back should always pay. A telling-off makes the next recall less likely.

stages.title: Coming back with mild distractions
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog comes back on a longer line when there is something mildly interesting around.
stages.whyItMatters: Real walks have smells, people and other dogs. Practising with small distractions first builds a recall that holds up outside.
stages.everydayPractice: On a long line, call once when the distraction is still far away, and reward generously when your dog comes.

gate.summary: Reliable recall on a 10 m long line with mild distraction. This does not unlock off-lead freedom in public.
gate.ownerCheck: On a 10 metre long line with something mildly interesting nearby, does {dog} come back when called once?

stages.ifGateFails: Make the distraction smaller or further away, or go back to the quiet place for a few days. Keep the long line on.
stages.maintenance: Keep the long line for new places. Off-lead only in secure areas you know, or with a trainer's advice.

lessons.title: A long line keeps it safe
lessons.body: Until {dog} reliably comes back, practise outside on a long line clipped to a harness. It lets them explore while you stay in control. Never use it to pull them towards you: if they don't come, guide gently or walk over and collect them.

lessons.title: Recall with something going on
lessons.aim: On the long line, call once while the distraction is still far away, and reward generously.

lessons.title: Small steps up
lessons.body: Add distance and distraction a little at a time. If {dog} stops coming back, make it easier for a few days: further from the distraction, closer to you, or a quieter place.

lessons.title: Pay recalls on walks
lessons.body: On today's walk, call {dog} back once or twice when nothing much is happening, reward them, and let them go back to sniffing. Coming back shouldn't always mean the fun ends.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: When is it right to let {dog} off the lead in an open space?
options: Once they came back three times today
When you're confident they'll come back when called, ideally somewhere secure first
Never, under any circumstances
lessons.explanation: Off-lead freedom waits until you're confident in their recall. Until then, a long line or a secure field keeps everyone safe.

title: Walking nicely on the lead
summary: From being comfortable on the lead to checking in with you on walks.

stages.title: Comfortable on the lead
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog is relaxed while the lead goes on and walks a few steps beside you at home.
stages.whyItMatters: A dog who is comfortable wearing the lead can start to learn where the reward is.
stages.everydayPractice: Clip the lead on for a moment at home, reward, and take it off again.

gate.summary: Stays relaxed while the lead is clipped on and walks a few steps beside you indoors.
gate.ownerCheck: At home, does {dog} stay relaxed while you clip the lead on, and walk a few steps beside you?

stages.ifGateFails: Keep the sessions very short, check the harness fits comfortably, and reward just for the lead going on.
stages.maintenance: Make the lead going on a calm, good moment before every walk.

lessons.title: A harness that fits
lessons.body: Choose a harness that doesn't sit across the front of {dog}'s shoulders, and fits so you can slip a finger under the straps. A comfortable dog learns; one who is pinched or rubbed just wants it off.

lessons.title: Small steps make it easy
lessons.body: Let {dog} sniff the harness and find treats around it, then feed a treat through the head hole before it ever goes on. Short, happy moments now save a lot of wriggling later.

lessons.title: Lead on, treat, lead off
lessons.aim: A few short rounds at home: clip the lead on, reward, walk a step or two, and take it off again.

lessons.title: A good moment before walks
lessons.body: Today, before you head out, clip the lead on calmly and give {dog} a treat as it goes on.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} backs away when the harness comes out. What helps most?
options: Hold them still and put it on quickly
Go back a step: treats around the harness, then through the head hole, before it goes on
Leave the harness on all day so they get used to it
lessons.explanation: Building it up in small, rewarding steps lets your dog choose to put their head in. Holding them still makes the harness something to avoid.

stages.title: A loose lead
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog walks beside you with the lead slack, starting somewhere quiet.
stages.whyItMatters: Pulling works when it gets your dog where they want to go. Stopping when the lead goes tight, and rewarding by your side, teaches that a loose lead is what gets them there.
stages.everydayPractice: On the first minutes of a walk, stop when the lead goes tight and move on when it's slack again.

gate.summary: Ten consecutive steps with a slack lead without you stopping.
gate.ownerCheck: Somewhere quiet, can {dog} walk ten steps in a row beside you with the lead slack?

stages.ifGateFails: Go back indoors or to the garden, reward more often at your side, and keep walks short and calm while you practise.
stages.maintenance: Reward walking at your side now and then on ordinary walks.

lessons.title: Why dogs pull
lessons.body: Pulling works when it gets {dog} where they want to go. So when the lead goes tight, stop and wait. The moment it goes slack, move on again. A loose lead becomes the thing that gets them there.

lessons.title: Stop and go
lessons.aim: Somewhere quiet: walk on while the lead is slack, stop when it goes tight, and reward {dog} at your side.

lessons.title: No quick fixes
lessons.body: Collars or leads that stop pulling by pinching or tightening are unpleasant for dogs and confusing, and they aren't needed. A comfortable harness and patience teach far more.

lessons.title: The first few minutes
lessons.body: Today, for the first few minutes of your walk, stop whenever the lead goes tight and move on as soon as it's slack.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: The lead goes tight as {dog} heads for a smell. What do you do?
options: Keep walking so they learn to keep up
Stop and wait, then move on when the lead is slack
Give the lead a quick tug
lessons.explanation: Stopping means pulling no longer gets your dog where they want to go. A slack lead does.

stages.title: Checking in on walks
stages.whatItMeans: On walks, your dog looks back at you from time to time without being asked.
stages.whyItMatters: A dog who checks in keeps the lead loose by choice and is easier to call when something comes up.
stages.everydayPractice: Carry a few treats and reward every time your dog looks back at you on a walk.

gate.summary: Checks in with you without a cue several times on a short, familiar walk.
gate.ownerCheck: On a familiar walk, does {dog} look back at you a few times without being asked?

stages.ifGateFails: Pick a quieter route, reward any glance your way, and use their name once if you need to.
stages.maintenance: Keep rewarding check-ins, especially in new places.

lessons.title: A glance is worth rewarding
lessons.body: When {dog} looks back at you on a walk without being asked, that's a check-in. Reward it, and they'll do it more often, which keeps the lead loose by their own choice.

lessons.title: Check-ins on a walk
lessons.aim: On a short, familiar walk: reward every time {dog} looks back at you.

lessons.title: Keep the lead relaxed
lessons.body: If something worries {dog} on a walk, keep the lead secure but loose and move further away. A tight lead can make a dog feel trapped, and a calmer dog can look back at you again.

lessons.title: Pocket a few treats
lessons.body: Today, carry a few small treats on your walk and reward each time {dog} looks back at you.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: On a walk, {dog} looks back at you for no reason. What's the best response?
options: Nothing, they didn't do anything
Reward them, it's a check-in
Ask them to sit first
lessons.explanation: Checking in is exactly what you want more of, so reward it the moment it happens.

title: Settling calmly at home
summary: From relaxing on a mat to settling while ordinary home life goes on.

stages.title: Relaxing on a mat
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog goes to a mat or bed and relaxes there for a short time while you are nearby.
stages.whyItMatters: A place that means rest gives your dog somewhere to switch off, and you a way to help them calm down.
stages.everydayPractice: Quietly drop a treat on the mat whenever your dog chooses to lie there.

gate.summary: Lies down on the mat and stays relaxed for about a minute in a quiet room.
gate.ownerCheck: In a quiet room, does {dog} lie down on their mat and stay relaxed for about a minute?

stages.ifGateFails: Practise after a walk or play, when your dog is already tired, and reward calm more often.
stages.maintenance: Keep the mat a good place: reward calm there now and then.

lessons.title: Calm can be learned
lessons.body: On a mat, reward {dog} for small signs of relaxing: lying down, a sigh, shifting their weight, resting their head. Bit by bit, the mat becomes a place to switch off.

lessons.title: Relax on the mat
lessons.aim: In a quiet room: put the mat down, wait, and calmly reward each sign of {dog} relaxing on it.

lessons.title: Say less, reward quietly
lessons.body: Let {dog} choose to relax rather than telling them again and again. When you reward, be calm and quiet: an excited voice can wake them right back up.

lessons.title: Catch them resting
lessons.body: Today, whenever {dog} chooses to lie on their mat or bed, quietly drop a treat there.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} lies on the mat and lets out a sigh. What do you do?
options: Quietly put a treat down by them
Praise them excitedly
Tell them to stay
lessons.explanation: A sigh is relaxing, which is exactly what you're rewarding. Keeping it calm helps them stay relaxed.

stages.title: Settling while life goes on
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog settles while you do ordinary things at home, like cooking or watching TV.
stages.whyItMatters: Most of a dog's day is at home. Being able to rest while the house is busy helps them cope with everything else.
stages.everydayPractice: While you have a cup of tea, reward your dog for lying quietly nearby.

gate.summary: Settles for a few minutes while you do something ordinary in the same room.
gate.ownerCheck: While you get on with something ordinary at home, does {dog} settle for a few minutes?

stages.ifGateFails: Pick a quieter moment and a shorter time, and make sure your dog has had enough exercise and sleep. A dog who can't settle at all may be unwell or worried: speak to your vet.
stages.maintenance: Give your dog quiet rest times every day, and protect their sleep.

lessons.title: Rest is part of training
lessons.body: Dogs need plenty of rest between walks, play and games. A dog who has had enough sleep finds it far easier to settle while the house is busy.

lessons.title: Settle while life goes on
lessons.aim: While you do something ordinary, like cooking or a cup of tea, reward {dog} for lying quietly nearby.

lessons.title: When they can't settle
lessons.body: Pacing, panting, yawning when not tired or licking their lips can mean {dog} is worried, not just restless. Give them a quiet space, and if it keeps happening or starts suddenly, talk to your vet.

lessons.title: A cup of tea together
lessons.body: Today, while you have a cup of tea, quietly reward {dog} for lying down nearby.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} keeps pacing and can't settle tonight, which isn't like them. What helps most?
options: Practise the settle for longer
Give them a quiet space, and talk to your vet if it carries on
Ignore it, they'll tire eventually
lessons.explanation: A sudden change can mean your dog is worried or unwell. Help them feel safe, and get it checked if it continues.

title: Greeting visitors calmly
summary: From four paws on the floor for a hello to waiting at the door when someone arrives.

stages.title: Four paws on the floor
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog keeps all four paws on the floor when someone they know says hello.
stages.whyItMatters: Jumping up is how many dogs say hello. Rewarding calm greetings shows them a better way that still gets attention.
stages.everydayPractice: When you come home, greet your dog only once all four paws are on the floor.

gate.summary: Keeps four paws on the floor while a familiar person says hello.
gate.ownerCheck: When someone {dog} knows says hello, do all four paws stay on the floor?

stages.ifGateFails: Ask people to greet more calmly and turn away if your dog jumps, and reward four paws on the floor straight away.
stages.maintenance: Everyone at home greets only calm paws on the floor.

lessons.title: Why dogs jump up
lessons.body: Jumping up is how many dogs say hello, and attention makes it worth doing again. Greet {dog} only when all four paws are on the floor, so calm is what gets the fuss.

lessons.title: Four paws for a hello
lessons.aim: With someone {dog} knows: say hello only while four paws are on the floor, and turn away calmly if they jump.

lessons.title: Everyone plays the same game
lessons.body: If one person cuddles {dog} when they jump, they'll keep trying. Ask family and friends to greet only four paws on the floor too.

lessons.title: When you come home
lessons.body: Today, when you get home, wait for four paws on the floor before you say hello.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} jumps up as a friend comes in. What should your friend do?
options: Push them down and say no
Turn away calmly, and say hello once four paws are down
Give them a cuddle to calm them down
lessons.explanation: Any attention, even pushing them down, can reward jumping. Turning away and greeting four paws teaches the better way to say hello.

stages.title: Waiting at the door
stages.whatItMeans: Your dog waits back from the door while it opens and a visitor comes in, until you say they can say hello.
stages.whyItMatters: The door is where greetings get exciting. Waiting there keeps everyone safe and gives your dog a calm start to the visit.
stages.everydayPractice: Before you open the door for a walk, wait for a calm moment, then open it as the reward.

gate.summary: Waits behind the door while it opens and a familiar visitor comes in, until released.
gate.ownerCheck: When a visitor {dog} knows comes in, does {dog} wait back from the door until you say they can say hello?

stages.ifGateFails: Practise the door with no one there first, or pop your dog behind a baby gate with something to chew while visitors arrive. If your dog seems worried rather than excited, give them space and get advice.
stages.maintenance: Keep the door calm: reward waiting, and use a gate on busy days.

lessons.title: Calm is what opens the door
lessons.body: The door is where greetings get exciting. Practise with no one there: wait for a calm moment, then open the door as the reward. Then a visitor's hello can be the reward for waiting back.

lessons.title: A short wait
lessons.aim: A few short rounds: ask {dog} to wait for a moment, then release and reward them.

lessons.title: Door manners
lessons.aim: At the front door with no one there: open it only while {dog} waits back, and close it calmly if they rush.

lessons.title: Excited or worried?
lessons.body: Some dogs rush the door because they're worried, not excited: look for lip licking, pinned ears or turning away. Give a worried dog a quiet space away from the door while visitors arrive, and get advice if it carries on.

lessons.title: Before every walk
lessons.body: Today, before you open the door for a walk, wait for a calm moment and let the door opening be the reward.

lessons.title: Quick check
lessons.question: {dog} hides and licks their lips when the doorbell rings. What helps most?
options: Make them greet the visitor so they get used to it
Give them a quiet space away from the door, and get advice if it carries on
Practise the door with more visitors
lessons.explanation: Those are signs of worry, not excitement. Space helps a worried dog feel safe; pushing them to greet can make it worse.
